forms.name: Self Assessment tax return
forms.what: This is the main HMRC Self Assessment tax return. It tells HMRC about your income so they can work out how much tax you owe.
doNext: Check the deadline on your letter or on GOV.UK. Online returns have a later deadline than paper ones.
Gather your income records before you start.
If you are not sure you need to send one, GOV.UK has a checker.
forms.watchOut: Late returns can lead to penalties, so do not leave it to the last day.

forms.name: Tax calculation letter (P800)
forms.what: This is a tax calculation letter from HMRC. It says you have paid too much or too little tax for a tax year.
doNext: Check the figures against what you know about your pay.
If it says you are owed money, follow the steps in the letter to claim it.
If it says you owe money, the letter explains how to pay.
forms.watchOut: These letters come by post. Be careful with emails, texts or calls about refunds, and do not use links in them. Sign in to GOV.UK yourself instead.

forms.name: End of year pay and tax summary (P60)
forms.what: A P60 is a yearly summary from your employer of your pay and the tax taken, for the tax year that ended on 5 April.
doNext: Keep it somewhere safe. You may need it to prove your income or to claim back overpaid tax.
If you lose it, ask your employer for a copy.
forms.watchOut: If you were working for your employer on 5 April, they should give you one by 31 May.

forms.name: Leaving a job form (P45)
forms.what: A P45 is given to you by your employer when you stop working for them. It shows your pay and tax so far in that tax year.
doNext: Keep Part 1A for your own records.
Give Parts 2 and 3 to your new employer, or to Jobcentre Plus if you are not working.
forms.watchOut: If you lose it, you cannot get a replacement. Your new employer can ask you to fill in a starter checklist instead.

forms.name: Company benefits form (P11D)
forms.what: A P11D tells you the value of company benefits your employer gave you, such as a company car or private medical insurance.
doNext: Check the benefits and values listed look right.
Keep it with your tax records.
forms.watchOut: You may not get one if your employer takes the tax on your benefits out of your pay.

forms.name: Starting a Personal Independence Payment (PIP) claim
detect: personal independence payment[\s\S]{0,80}(new claim|start your claim)
forms.what: This is the first step of a claim for Personal Independence Payment (PIP), a benefit for extra costs caused by a long-term health condition or disability. It asks basic questions about you.
doNext: Fill in the basic details and send the form back by the date shown.
You will then be sent a second, longer form called "How your disability affects you". That one matters most.
Start collecting letters or lists from your doctor, nurse or care team now. They can be used as evidence.
forms.watchOut: In England and Wales the claim usually starts by phone to the PIP new claims line. In Scotland you apply for Adult Disability Payment instead.

forms.name: PIP form: How your disability affects you (PIP2)
forms.what: This is the main PIP form. It asks how your health condition or disability affects everyday things like preparing food, washing, getting around and being with other people. The answers decide whether you get PIP and how much.
doNext: Return it, or finish it online, within one month of the date it was sent.
Answer for your worst days and for how things usually are, not your best day. Give real examples.
Attach any evidence you have, such as a care plan, prescription list or letter from your doctor.
If you need more time or help, contact the PIP enquiry line before the deadline.
forms.watchOut: Missing the deadline can mean your claim is stopped. Keep a copy of everything you send.

forms.name: PIP award review form (AR1)
detect: award review[\s\S]{0,60}how your disability affects you
forms.what: This is a review of a PIP award you already have. DWP uses it to check whether your needs have changed. Your answers can change what you get.
doNext: Return it by the date on the letter.
Describe how things are now, with real examples, even if nothing has changed.
Attach new evidence if you have it, such as a recent letter from your doctor.
forms.watchOut: If you do not return it, your PIP can be stopped. Ask for more time before the date if you need it.

forms.name: Capability for work questionnaire (ESA50)
forms.what: DWP sends this questionnaire to find out how your health condition or disability affects your ability to work. The answers help decide whether you get Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) and what kind.
doNext: Return it by the date on the letter. Ask for more time before that date if you need it.
Describe how you manage on your worst days, with specific examples. Say if tasks hurt, take longer, or you need help.
Attach evidence from your doctor or care team if you have it. Keep a copy of everything.
forms.watchOut: If you do not return it without a good reason, your benefit can be stopped.

forms.name: Mandatory reconsideration request (CRMR1)
forms.what: This form asks DWP to look again at a benefit decision you think is wrong. It is the step you usually need to take before you can appeal to a tribunal.
doNext: Send it, with any evidence, to the address at the top of your decision letter.
You usually need to ask within one month of the date on the decision. You can ask later if you have a good reason.
Explain clearly why you think the decision is wrong. Keep a copy and note the date you sent it.
You will get a new letter (a mandatory reconsideration notice). If you still disagree, you can appeal.
forms.watchOut: Do not wait. The one-month limit is easy to miss.

forms.name: Appeal to the benefits tribunal (SSCS1)
detect: appeal to the social security (and child support )?tribunal
forms.what: This form is used to appeal a benefit decision to an independent tribunal. You normally do this after you have asked DWP for a mandatory reconsideration and still disagree.
doNext: Include the mandatory reconsideration notice. The tribunal usually needs it.
You normally have to appeal within one month of the date on that notice. Check the letter for the exact date.
Say what you disagree with and why. Add evidence if you have it.
Keep a copy and note the date you sent it.
forms.watchOut: A late appeal may be refused. If you are close to the deadline, send it and explain why it is late.

forms.name: Appointee application (BF56)
forms.what: This DWP form is used to apply to become someone's appointee. An appointee manages a person's benefits for them when the person cannot do it themselves.
doNext: The person applying must give their own details and the details of the person they will act for.
Send it back to the address on the form.
DWP may contact the person or others to check the arrangement.
Keep a copy.
forms.watchOut: An appointee must act in the person's best interests and keep records of how the money is used.

forms.name: Carer's Allowance claim (DS700)
forms.what: This is a claim for Carer's Allowance, money for people who spend at least 35 hours a week caring for someone who gets certain disability benefits.
doNext: Check the person you care for gets a qualifying disability benefit.
Fill in your details, the details of the person you care for, and your work or study.
You can usually claim online as well as on paper.
forms.watchOut: Your claim can affect benefits that the person you care for gets, so check first. Tell DWP if your circumstances change.

forms.name: Attendance Allowance claim (AA1A)
forms.what: This is a claim for Attendance Allowance, which helps people over State Pension age who need help with personal care because of a health condition or disability.
doNext: Fill in the form about the help you need, day and night.
Describe your worst days with real examples.
Send it back to the address on the form. Keep a copy.
forms.watchOut: It is not means tested, so savings do not affect it. It can affect other benefits, so ask an adviser if you are unsure.

forms.name: Disability Living Allowance for children (DLA)
forms.what: Disability Living Allowance (DLA) now only covers children under 16 in England and Wales. It helps with extra costs when a child has a disability or health condition.
doNext: Describe how your child's needs differ from other children of the same age.
Give real examples of care and supervision they need.
Attach reports from doctors, therapists or school if you have them.
forms.watchOut: Adults moved to Personal Independence Payment (PIP). In Scotland the child benefit is called Child Disability Payment.

forms.name: Child Benefit claim (CH2)
forms.what: This is a claim for Child Benefit, a payment for people bringing up a child under 16, or under 20 in approved education or training.
doNext: Claim as soon as you can, because it can only be backdated for a short time.
You will need the child's birth certificate or other proof, and your own details.
Send it to the address on the form, or claim online.
forms.watchOut: A higher earner in the household may have to pay some of it back through the tax system, but claiming is still worth doing.

forms.name: Guardian's Allowance claim (BG1)
forms.what: Guardian's Allowance is extra money if you are bringing up a child whose parents have died, and in some other cases.
doNext: You must already be getting Child Benefit for the child.
Fill in the form with details of the child and the child's parents.
Keep a copy and send supporting papers such as death certificates if asked.
forms.watchOut: It is claimed on top of Child Benefit, not instead of it.

forms.name: Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit claim (BI100A / BI100PD)
forms.what: This is a claim for money if you were hurt in an accident at work, or developed a disease because of your job.
doNext: Fill in details of the accident or the disease, and your work history.
Give dates, places and names of employers.
You may be asked to attend a medical assessment.
forms.watchOut: The deadlines and rules differ for an accident and for a disease. Check the form notes.

forms.name: Maternity Allowance claim (MA1)
forms.what: This is a claim for Maternity Allowance, money for pregnant people who cannot get Statutory Maternity Pay, for example because they are self-employed or have changed jobs.
doNext: Fill in your details, your work history and your due date.
Send proof of your pregnancy, such as a MATB1 certificate, and proof of earnings if asked.
You can claim from about 26 weeks into your pregnancy.
forms.watchOut: Claim as early as you can so you do not lose any payments.

forms.name: NHS Low Income Scheme claim (HC1)
forms.what: This form asks for help with NHS costs such as prescriptions, dental treatment, glasses and travel to hospital, if you are on a low income.
doNext: Fill in details of your income, savings and living costs.
Send proof if the form asks for it.
You will get a certificate that shows what help you can get.
forms.watchOut: The rules are different in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Do not claim free help unless you are sure you qualify.

forms.name: Pension Credit
forms.what: Pension Credit tops up your weekly income if you have reached State Pension age and have a low income. It can also open the door to other help, such as help with housing costs and the Warm Home Discount.
doNext: Check on the official site whether you might qualify.
Have your income, savings and bank details ready.
Claim by phone, online or post. You can claim up to three months back if you qualify.
forms.watchOut: Never pay someone to claim it for you. It is free to claim.

forms.name: Statutory Sick Pay (SSP)
forms.what: Statutory Sick Pay is money your employer pays while you are too ill to work. The SSP1 form is given to people who cannot get it, to help them claim other benefits.
doNext: Tell your employer you are sick, following their usual rules.
Keep any fit note from your doctor.
If you get an SSP1 form, keep it. You may need it when you claim other benefits.
forms.watchOut: Check your contract too, since some employers pay more than SSP.

forms.name: Warm Home Discount
forms.what: The Warm Home Discount is a one-off amount taken off your electricity bill during the winter if you qualify. Many people get it automatically.
doNext: Check your energy supplier's letter or email. You may not need to do anything.
If you are asked to apply, do it only through your supplier or the official site.
Keep any reference number from your supplier.
forms.watchOut: Scammers pretend to offer it. Never give your bank details to someone who contacts you out of the blue.

forms.name: Healthy Start
forms.what: Healthy Start helps pregnant people and families with children under 4 who get certain benefits to buy basic foods, milk and vitamins.
doNext: Apply online on the Healthy Start site, or ask a midwife or health visitor to help.
You may need proof of pregnancy or your child's details.
The money goes on a prepaid card.
forms.watchOut: You do not have to pay anything to apply.

forms.name: Widowed Parent's Allowance
forms.what: Widowed Parent's Allowance can be paid if your husband, wife or civil partner died before 6 April 2017 and you have a dependent child. For deaths from 6 April 2017, Bereavement Support Payment is used instead.
doNext: Check the date of the death on the form notes.
Fill in details of you, your partner who died and your children.
Send it with the documents it asks for.
forms.watchOut: It can be backdated only for a short time, so claim as soon as you can.

forms.name: Warwickshire widow(er) or partner pension
forms.what: This is about a pension paid by the Warwickshire Pension Fund to a surviving husband, wife, civil partner or sometimes partner of a member who has died.
doNext: Tell the pension fund about the death as soon as you can.
Have the death certificate and your marriage or civil partnership certificate ready.
Send the form and the documents it asks for to the address on it.
forms.watchOut: The rules depend on the member's membership dates and your relationship. Contact the pension fund if you are unsure.

forms.name: Housing Benefit
forms.what: Housing Benefit helps with rent for people on a low income. Most people of working age now claim help with housing costs through Universal Credit instead.
doNext: Check which one applies to you. Your council can tell you.
Gather proof of your income, savings, rent and who lives with you.
Return the form with the documents it asks for by the date shown.
forms.watchOut: Tell the council quickly if your income, rent or household changes.

forms.name: Council Tax Reduction
forms.what: Council Tax Reduction is a discount on your Council Tax bill if you are on a low income or get certain benefits. It is run by your local council, so the rules differ by area.
doNext: Check your council's website or the form notes for what you need.
Gather proof of your income, savings and who lives with you.
Send the form back by the date shown.
forms.watchOut: Keep paying your Council Tax until the council tells you your reduction has been agreed.

forms.name: Disabled Students' Allowance (DSA)
forms.what: Disabled Students' Allowance helps with extra study costs caused by a disability, mental health condition, long-term health condition or learning difference such as dyslexia.
doNext: Apply through Student Finance, with the DSA form that applies to you.
You will need evidence of your condition, for example a letter from your doctor or an assessment report.
After approval you may be asked to have a needs assessment.
forms.watchOut: It is separate from your tuition and living cost loans and does not have to be paid back.

forms.name: UK Global Health Insurance Card (GHIC / EHIC)
forms.what: The UK Global Health Insurance Card (GHIC) or European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) gives access to state-provided healthcare when you travel to some countries. It is free from the NHS.
doNext: Apply only on the official NHS site.
You will need your name, date of birth and NHS or National Insurance number.
The card usually lasts five years. It can be renewed in the last months of validity.
forms.watchOut: Some websites charge a fee for a free card. Do not pay anyone to apply.

forms.name: Jobseeker's Allowance (JSA)
forms.what: Jobseeker's Allowance is money for people who are out of work or working very few hours and who are looking for work. New Style JSA depends on your National Insurance record.
doNext: Check you are able to work and are looking for work.
Have your National Insurance number, bank details and employment history ready.
Go to any interviews or appointments you are given, and keep a record of your job searches.
forms.watchOut: You can claim Universal Credit instead. Ask which is better for you.

forms.name: UK passport application
forms.what: This is an application to get, renew or replace a UK passport.
doNext: Apply online if you can, as it is usually quicker and cheaper.
Have a photo that meets the passport photo rules, and your old passport if you have one.
Check the processing time before you book travel.
forms.watchOut: Only use the official government site. Other sites may charge you more.

forms.name: Driving licence application
forms.what: This is an application to get, renew or change a driving licence, from the DVLA.
doNext: Apply online if you can. It is usually quicker.
You will need ID, your address history for the last three years, your National Insurance number and a photo.
If you have a medical condition that affects driving, you must tell the DVLA.
forms.watchOut: Only use the official DVLA site. Other sites may charge extra fees.

forms.name: Visa and immigration forms
forms.what: This is a Home Office form or letter about a visa, leave to remain or another immigration application.
doNext: Check the date by which you must respond or apply. Immigration deadlines are strict.
Gather the documents it asks for, with certified translations if needed.
Keep copies of everything you send and your reference number.
forms.watchOut: Only use the official government site. Never pay someone who contacts you offering a visa. For advice, use a regulated immigration adviser.

forms.name: ADHD or autism questionnaire
forms.what: This is a questionnaire used by a health service as part of looking at whether a full ADHD or autism assessment is appropriate. It does not give a diagnosis.
doNext: Answer honestly about how you usually are, and how you have been for a long time, not just this week.
Give examples where there is space.
If it asks about childhood, a family member or old school reports may help.
Keep a copy and take it to your appointment.
forms.watchOut: If a question is unclear, ask the service that sent it. There are no trick questions.
